speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members have asked several questions regarding these cases.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After that, Minister Chan Chun Sing will address the more detailed questions in his Statement.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On 5 July, the Director of CPIB briefed me on the findings he had at that point.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He told me that CPIB would need to interview Minister Iswaran to take the investigation further and he sought my concurrence to open a formal investigation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I gave my concurrence the next day, on 6 July.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On 11 July, Minister Iswaran was brought in by CPIB and subsequently, released on bail.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I instructed him to take leave of absence until the investigations were completed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Such incidents involving Ministers are rare and there is no rule or precedent on how to effect an interdiction on a political office holder.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Hence, I used the current Civil Service practice as a reference point.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The specific details in Minister Iswaran's case follow generally how the Civil Service would deal with a senior officer in a similar situation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But this was my decision as Prime Minister, because the political contexts for a Minister and a civil servant being investigated and interdicted are different.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I should point out that CPIB investigations are still ongoing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am unable to provide more details on the case so as not to prejudice the investigations in any way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I ask Members of this House and the public to refrain from speculation and conjecture.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must allow CPIB to do its work, to investigate the matter fully, thoroughly and independently.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the investigation is completed, CPIB will submit its findings to the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC), which will decide what to do with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whichever way the facts come out, the case will be taken to its logical conclusion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Next, on the resignations of former Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin and former Member of Parliament (MP) Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were both spoken to and counselled, separately.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They both said they would stop the affair.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But as it turned out, they did not.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most recently in February 2023, I spoke to them again, separately.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Tan admitted that what he did was wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I accepted but I told him that before he actually resigned, I had first to make sure residents in Kembangan-Chai Chee, his ward, and Marine Parade, his Group Representation Constituency (GRC) were taken care of.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Meanwhile, his relationship with Miss Cheng had to stop.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have been asked – why did I take so long, more than two years, to act?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In retrospect, and certainly now, knowing how things eventually turned out, I agree.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But let me explain my general approach as well as my thinking at that point in time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These sorts of relationships happen from time to time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have happened in the past and no doubt will happen again in the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In such cases, what we do depends on many factors: the circumstances, how inappropriate or scandalous the behaviour was, the family situations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also have to be conscious of the impact on innocent parties, particularly the spouses and children.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I had explained this at my press conference on 20 July and so did Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong last week in a BBC interview.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is not a new position; it reflects the PAP's long-standing practice, since the days of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no single template that applies to all extramarital affairs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But there can be at least three situations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The first situation is where the individuals involved will be talked to, and if they stop, the matter ends there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The second situation is where immediate action has to be taken.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, when one party has supervisory power over the other party, and we have in the past taken immediate action, in a few cases.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The third situation, where the relationship raises some questions of propriety, beyond it being an extramarital affair per se.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The parties will be talked to, but the matter cannot end there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even if the affair stops, some action has to follow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But what that action is and when it is taken, depends on the nature of the facts and the boundaries that have been transgressed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The present situation falls into the third category.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Tan and Miss Cheng had to stop their affair.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In deciding what more should be done, consider this: would we object to having the Speaker being married to a Member of Parliament (MP)?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Would we object to having the Speaker being married to an MP?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think the answer is no – that would be perfectly alright.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no direct reporting line between the Speaker and an MP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thus, an open, legitimate relationship between the Speaker and an MP is not in itself objectionable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Hence, this situation of the Speaker having an affair with an MP does not fall into the category where immediate action has to be taken.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: However, the Speaker has some official capacity vis-à-vis MPs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: An extramarital affair between him and an MP is therefore problematic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It puts other MPs and staff in an awkward position, and it is just not proper.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After I spoke to Mr Tan in November 2020, he told me that the relationship would end.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I, therefore, felt there was some leeway to take some time to decide what further steps to take.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In this context, the possible actions that could have followed were on the basis that the extramarital affair had stopped, I would have asked Mr Tan to step down as Speaker some time before the end of the term, but in a way which would reduce the public embarrassment to him and his family.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As to whether one or both should also resign as Members – I had not decided at that time, but quite likely, both would have had to leave at some point.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By giving the matter some time, I had hoped to give them a softer exit, and save them and their families the pain and embarrassment that they are suffering now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I placed much weight on protecting their families; perhaps too much.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Likewise, for the case involving a former Member across the aisle, in the Workers' Party (WP).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hope that MPs and the public can empathise and have compassion for the families and give them the privacy and space they need to heal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The way we have handled these incidents shows how seriously the PAP takes our responsibility of governing Singapore and being accountable to Parliament and to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The investigation reports were tabled in Parliament, and we had a long session answering MPs’ questions in this House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When CPIB discovered, on its own, that it had reason to arrest and interview a Minister, it opened a formal investigation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: CPIB came across something that needed investigating and proceeded to do their job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the Speaker of Parliament and a Government MP fell short of the standards of propriety and personal conduct expected of them, they were asked to resign.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We took some time to sort it out, probably longer than we should have, but we did what we needed to do and put the situation right.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The two CPIB investigations, and the response to the personal misconduct case, show two aspects of how this PAP Government works.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Two, when people slip in their personal lives, the PAP will look at the facts of each case carefully and deal with the matter as humanely and sensitively as possible, according to the principles that the party has established.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In any system, however comprehensive the safeguards, sometimes something will still go wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The PAP Government does our utmost to minimise that possibility.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We work hard to identify the right people to bring into politics and appoint into responsible positions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We vet them carefully, test and stretch them, before entrusting them with heavier responsibilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Often, they measure up, but sometimes they fall short.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Occasionally, they transgress the norms of conduct, or commit wrongdoing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All these cases were handled by Mr Lee Kuan Yew who was then Prime Minister – thoroughly, transparently, and applying the full force of the law.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is still how the PAP Government deals with such cases.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has not changed under my charge; and it would not under my successor either.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the People’s Action Party (PAP) has always maintained an honest and clean Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A clean Government and good governance are critical to our democracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, we have strict laws in place to check on corruption.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On values and personal integrity, we expect Ministers and Members of Parliament (MPs) to meet social norms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Singapore, while corruption cases involving political leaders are rare, it has still happened before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is because even the most comprehensive safeguards can still go wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they also reflect our determination to stand for honesty and against corruption.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We firmly believe that to maintain an honest political system and for the people to continue to trust the PAP, we must deal with issues transparently.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, when anyone, including Ministers or MPs, are involved in corruption or illegal behaviour, there is zero tolerance, and we will investigate fully.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the investigation finds that there was no wrongdoing or conflict of interest, the matter would be closed and those involved exonerated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the investigation shows that there is misconduct, they would be dealt with the full force of the law.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In terms of personal conduct, the PAP expects the Ministers and MPs to hold themselves to the highest standards and to be self-disciplined.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: However, when people slip up in their personal lives, circumstances differ and we have to look at the facts case by case, and deal with each of them individually.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, I had hoped they would end their affair because their families would suffer the most if the affair was exposed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Indeed, my most important consideration throughout was how this would affect their families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If they had ended the affair, they need not have left politics under these embarrassing circumstances and hurt their families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Regrettably, they did not deal with it properly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In any extramarital affair, the families are affected and hurt greatly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whether it is a case involving the PAP or the WP, I hope everyone would give the families time and privacy to heal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We cannot guarantee that this sort of incident would never happen again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it does, we will continue to deal with it in accordance with the PAP’s principles.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My team and I are very clear about the importance of keeping our politics clean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As we have always done, we will continue to exercise self-discipline and uphold the principles of integrity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is the promise of the PAP Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, let me assure Singaporeans that we will protect the integrity of our system of Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I will not flinch or hesitate to do my duty, to keep our system robust and clean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is how the PAP Government can continue to deserve the trust that Singaporeans have placed in us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have spoken often about how precious trust is and how crucial it is for our democracy to work well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The founding generation built up Singapore and entrusted it to our generation in good shape.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is incumbent on us to protect and uphold this system, to keep it incorruptible and clean, and maintain high standards of propriety.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing will be making a related Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will allow clarifications to be raised on both Statements after the Statement by Minister Chan.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Other parties, including Ministers, defer to the judgement of these agencies, and do not and should not independently release such information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Those familiar with how law enforcement agencies operate, including CPIB, will know how they usually make their announcements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The standard practice is that agencies do not disclose the names of persons who are being investigated or arrested.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Say someone has been picked up, arrested, and investigations are ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If it is immediately announced that the person has been arrested and is being investigated, it may prejudice the person.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The impression that he has done wrong will be there, even if subsequent investigations do not result in any charges being brought against him.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Thus, to be fair to the persons involved, law enforcement agencies generally refrain from immediately naming the persons being investigated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are situations where agencies will depart from this norm and mention names.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At that point, CPIB did not state that Minister Iswaran had been arrested, as it had wanted to first establish more facts of the case, including hearing his side of the story.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What law enforcement agencies, including CPIB, reveal at any point in time takes into account their operational considerations in the cases they deal with – including preserving the integrity of evidence, protecting the confidentiality of ongoing investigations and avoiding impact on other related parties.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is why the Prime Minister’s initial statement and Deputy Prime Minister’s doorstop interview on 12 July took reference from CPIB’s press release on the same day.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This was the proper thing to do because Ministers, including the Prime Minister, should not reveal more than what the law enforcement agencies are prepared to disclose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While Ministers do have the final decision-making power, they will usually take the advice of the law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Two days later, on 14 July, Hotel Properties Limited (HPL) issued a statement saying that Mr Ong Beng Seng had been "given a notice of arrest" by CPIB.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: By then, investigations had been ongoing for three days and CPIB had obtained more facts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Some Members – Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Gerald Giam and Ms He Ting Ru – have asked about the considerations for timely and mandatory disclosure of information about a political office holder who is under investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The primary considerations are what I have just outlined.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In due course, further details of the investigations will be made public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But I hope we can all recognise that we must give CPIB the time and space they need to do their work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This was a case that CPIB had uncovered by themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can rely on CPIB to conduct its investigations thoroughly and independently, and to see this case to its logical conclusion – as it has with every other case it has investigated over 70 years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Iswaran has not been charged, much less convicted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members should, therefore, avoid speculating on or prejudicing the outcome of the investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai and Mr Louis Chua asked whether all CPIB investigations require the Prime Minister's concurrence and if CPIB is obliged to seek the Prime Minister's concurrence to open formal investigations of potential offences that CPIB has uncovered.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While CPIB reports directly to the Prime Minister, it is functionally independent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: CPIB does not require the Prime Minister's concurrence to conduct its investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Prime Minister concurred within a day of receiving the Director of CPIB's report.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In reality, we have never had a Prime Minister who has impeded CPIB's work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I should also remind Members there are Constitutional safeguards for the appointment or removal of the Director of CPIB, which require the concurrence of the President.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There were also several queries by Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Leong Mun Wai seeking more details on CPIB's investigation findings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members must remember that this is an ongoing investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Therefore, I am unable to disclose further details at this juncture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is to ensure that the investigations are not jeopardised and affected individuals or entities are not prejudiced.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the Ridout Road bungalows matter, the two Ministers had asked the Prime Minister for an independent investigation into their rental of the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) black and white bungalows and the Prime Minister had tasked CPIB to do the investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Prime Minister had no reason to believe that the Ministers had committed any wrongdoing then and, therefore, saw no need to put them on leave of absence during the investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Prime Minister could have asked the Ministers to take leave of absence should evidence have surfaced during the investigations that warranted it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the case involving Minister Iswaran, CPIB came across some information concerning him while investigating a separate matter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It then decided it should look further into the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked whether Minister Iswaran's gazetted leave of absence from his duties from 7 July to 9 July was related to the CPIB investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the record, Minister Iswaran took leave of absence from 7 July to 9 July for personal matters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat covered his duties during that period.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, on the Code of Conduct for Ministers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked if there will be a review of the Code.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Code sets out the principles and rules on how Ministers should act and conduct their personal affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will continue to review and update the Code of Conduct for Ministers regularly, taking into account evolving circumstances and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, the Government recently announced that going forward, officers with access to privileged information that can influence the outcomes of decisions related to state-owned properties must make a declaration before they can rent Government properties managed by their agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The same would apply to political office holders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service Code of Conduct sets out the principles and rules that public officers must abide by.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is periodically refreshed to ensure that the integrity and high standards of the Public Service are upheld.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the course of their work, public officers may come across different requests, be it from colleagues, friends, members of the public or political office holders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When handling these requests, officers are expected to maintain a high level of professionalism and safeguard the confidentiality of official information as well as the political impartiality of the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Should an officer be unsure of a request because it seems inappropriate or unrelated to official work, he should consult and seek guidance from his supervisor.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If the request comes from his supervisor or a more senior officer, the officer can escalate the matter appropriately through the chain of command, including directly to his Permanent Secretary, the Head of Agency, the Head of Civil Service or the Minister-in-charge of the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Code of Conduct is reinforced through various channels, such as annual quizzes, declarations, induction programmes for new entrants, milestone programmes and regular Service-wide reminders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is an established Internal Disclosure Policy framework within the Civil Service where officers can report any wrongful practices that they have observed in their Ministries to their Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All reports are treated with utmost confidentiality and every effort is made to protect the officer's identity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is a non-retaliation clause to further protect the interests of the officer who made the report.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If a report is made in good faith, no action will be taken against the reporting officer even if the investigation finds no wrongful practice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Between 2020 and 2022, no report which surfaced through this channel was referred to the CPIB for investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In addition, there is a Public Service Protocol for the Reporting of Corruption.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Under this protocol, public officers are expected to directly report to the Police or the CPIB at the earliest opportunity when they learn of any act of corruption or have reason to believe that such an act may have been committed in their Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The identity of the person making the report will be kept confidential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is provided for under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: CPIB treats all reports received seriously, whether the complainant is named or anonymous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Public sector cases form a small portion of the cases CPIB investigates each year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In 2022, four public sector officers were prosecuted in Court for offences investigated by CPIB.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about the rules for declaring meal invitations and the threshold values for doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The rules for the Civil Service on accepting gifts and hospitality are designed to maintain incorruptibility and to prevent officers from becoming beholden to any person or organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Civil servants must declare to their Permanent Secretaries any gifts they receive from external stakeholders on account of their official position or work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the course of their work, officers may be invited to meals by local or foreign stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They may accept when there are legitimate work-related reasons or when it is impractical or impolite to reject the meal.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Unlike gifts, it is more difficult to ascertain the value of a meal.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is especially if they assess that the value of the meal or hospitality is incongruent with the professional nature of the meeting and may give rise to perceptions of influence peddling and conflict of interest, real or perceived.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I should share with this House that civil servants are sensitised on these matters that even when they receive gifts of fruits or sweets – as is customary on many of our festive occasions – such gifts are usually distributed in the agency or to a community organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Political office holders adopt a similar spirit and principles in their official activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are specific rules spelt out in the Annex of the Code of Conduct for Ministers on the acceptance of gifts and services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If the return of the gift is impractical, the gift must be handed over to the political office holder's Ministry to be dealt with in accordance with official guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Otherwise, the gifts have to be surrendered to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Should the queries be sufficiently addressed, it may not be necessary for Members to pose identical Parliamentary Questions for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have two buckets of clarification – first, with regard to the standards of the PAP that the Prime Minister spoke of; and second, with regard to the circumstances involving the departure of the former Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin and former MP Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly with regard to what the Prime Minister knew and what the Prime Minister did about it over a period of almost three years before coming clean on the matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will give three examples that capture this point, and my clarifications will be contained therein.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 23 May, the Prime Minister released the statement stating Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean had been appointed to establish whether there had been any wrongdoing in the Ridout Road rentals in order to maintain the highest standards of integrity in Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public came to know about the CPIB investigation more than a month later when investigations were completed, with CPIB confirming no criminal offence was disclosed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a parallel universe, Sir, there is a perception that if a Singaporean or Singaporean company took such a cavalier and breezy approach with critical facts under today's PAP, they can expect to receive a Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation (POFMA) direction from a PAP Minister for perpetuating false statements of fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has the Prime Minister inquired with the CPIB why it undertook such a course of action that brought unnecessary attention to the CPIB's processes and, by extension, even its impartiality, involving the release of statements in the public interest?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If he did not, would he consider to do so?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, during COVID-19, the public was belatedly informed by a Minister in this House, that his senior Cabinet colleagues were aware by October 2020 that previous Government assurances on TraceTogether being solely used for contact tracing were effectively false statements of fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Misrepresentations had hitherto been made by various Government Ministers and possibly in this House even, before October 2020, and they stood uncorrected for months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike as represented by the Prime Minister, these are not events that I quote, "are clustered together", all coming at one go.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead, they reveal a pattern of behaviour over a period of time of the PAP engaging in half-truths on matters of significant public interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And this behaviour goes a long way to explain why there is real disquiet among Singaporeans today when the PAP invokes the memory of Pioneer Generation PAP leaders and talks about trust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I invite the Prime Minister to reconsider his position in view of the PAP's pattern of behaviour in this term of Government, especially when a potentially embarrassing issue comes up?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would not their being on the same Committee have resulted in more interactions between them than necessary or given official reasons to be together?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My next question: the Prime Minister stated at the press conference in response to a reporter's question that, I quote, "as for comparison with Michael Palmer, I think it depends on the situation of the case and I said you've got to look at the circumstances, spouses, the family's condition and how you manage this as sensitively as you can and yet do your duty, and it depends on the person's response as well as the specifics, so I don't think it's possible to make direct comparisons".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Prime Minister's reference to such sensitivity, an eminently reasonable approach to take with delicate matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the PAP selectively applies these standards, expecting Singaporeans to give the PAP the full benefit of doubt when its MPs foul up, while screaming blue murder when the Opposition seek to make the same point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When former MP Raeesah Khan revealed to the WP leaders that she was a rape victim, sensitivity was not even considered by the Committee of Privileges in accounting for the delay in addressing Raeesah's lies to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the Prime Minister did not bat an eyelid in giving the Leader of the Opposition a sermon on Confucian ethics, morality and shame, even though at the material time, he would have been aware of the affair between Speaker Tan Chuan-Jin and Member of Parliament Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If he had stepped down as Speaker, could he still not have continued as a Marine Parade MP until the arrangements were made?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And before I round off, Mr Speaker, just one additional question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Did he personally counsel them and how often did he check in on the status of the relationship thereafter?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I ask Prime Minister to respond, I have given Leader of the Opposition some leeway.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At this stage, we should be asking clarifications and not make speeches.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I request Members, going forward, to remember that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Leader of the Opposition raises three issues, one of which has been extensively debated, in fact, in 2020, during COVID-19; and I do not need to go back there again, which is the TraceTogether and whether we should have announced earlier when we discovered that the Police were using it for their purposes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think that has been completely explained, closed; that matter is done.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And the CPIB does not reveal that investigation generally until it has reason to believe that this investigation has to carry on, that it has to go somewhere.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, in general, CPIB investigations are not, in the first instance, announced at all.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the case of the 12 July statement, the reason why the CPIB said exactly what they said, if you listen carefully to Minister Chan Chun Sing, that explanation has been given – which was that they had to say what they felt justified in saying at that point for operational reasons and to be fair to the persons involved, and the Ministers, unless we have strong reason to do otherwise, we will go along and we will not go beyond what the CPIB needs and is able to say.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I think in terms of the transmission of information, we are pursuing a red herring.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We could equally well ask, for example, when did the Leader of Opposition know about problems in his party and what did he do about them?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But those are matters which the WP will have to decide and will have to account for to Singaporeans, and the PAP, we establish our own standards and we establish our own practices.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As for the relationship between Tan Chuan-Jin and Cheng Li Hui and the questions on the House Committee and foreign trips, I think I will leave that to Leader to answer subsequently.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On the difference between this case and the case of Michael Palmer and the PA staff, I think there are two differences.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: One, in Michael Palmer's case, it involved a PA staff who worked in a team which supported Michael Palmer and other GRA advisors in Pasir Ris-Punggol GRC, subsequently Pasir Ris-Punggol GRC and Punggol East Single Member Constituency (SMC).

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not wish to go into specifics of how the extramarital affairs are different, but suffice to say, they were different.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As for Raeesah Khan, that raises many issues and those issues have been exhaustively debated in the Committee of Privileges.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The matter, further problems were recorded and reported by the Committee of Privileges and the matter has been referred to the Police for investigations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I would leave that to the Police to pursue the matter and take it where it may.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As for the time, why I took so long, I counselled Tan Chuan-Jin at the beginning.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I saw to it that Cheng Li Hui was also counselled at the beginning.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not wish to go beyond that and to delve into the ins and outs of how it happened but suffice to say, eventually it came to a break point and did not stop, and they had to go.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And we brought it out and we are open about it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And when I was asked, I said, yes, I knew sometime after GE 2020 – which is November 2020.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If I had not said that, nobody would know that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And therefore, we clear the matter and I think we account to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Working trips would be, for example, for the Olympic Games and so on.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of the five official overseas trips, only one was where Miss Cheng Li Hui was present as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That was the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly (AIPA) General Assembly trip to Cambodia in 2022.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There were 15 MP delegates in total for this trip.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I understand that the Parliament Secretariat had, since 2020, organised 18 overseas Parliamentary trips, including the AIPA General Assembly one in August, the upcoming one in 2023; and 60 MPs have participated in these visits across the years since 2020.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Of the 18 visits, Miss Cheng Li Hui only participated in one overseas trip and that is the AIPA General Assembly one held in Cambodia in 2022, but she did not attend more overseas trips than other MPs.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With regard to her selection for that trip, I understand that the name was put up by the staffing officer and approved.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With respect to the House Committee, there are several Standing Select Committees.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The names for the composition of the Committees are put forward, in the case of the PAP representation, by myself.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: After the last General Election, I had sought Leader of the Opposition's nominations for the Opposition MPs, because the rules provide that for Standing Select Committees, the proportion of the ratio of majority MPs and Opposition MPs should be roughly the proportion that they are represented in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first point is a point of order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I respect what Speaker mentioned about not making extended speeches, but I was merely doing exactly what had transpired about one month ago when PAP MPs made extended speeches, specifically the Prime Minister, in the course of a Ministerial Statement in response to a question, I believe from backbencher Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I do seek your indulgence, Speaker, I was not going anything beyond what was already carried out by a PAP MP in the course of a Ministerial Statement last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand what Standing Order 23 says, I understand that a debate is not to ensue and they cannot be more than clarifications, but nothing special was undertaken by me in the course of me asking questions just now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just want to put that on record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In terms of the Prime Minister's replies, I think some of them still do not go into the details of matters that Singaporeans are actually quite concerned about, but I will address some responses which the Prime Minister gave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: First, on TraceTogether, that this has been extensively debated and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This was in a The Straits Times article on 14 March, well after we had discussed TraceTogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Prime Minister came out to say, "I think we made a mistake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Prime Minister spoke about the Leader of the Opposition – what I did, what I knew.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I had handled this in the course of my press conference where I took 12 questions: when did the affair start; what information I had secured from the parties concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the Prime Minister has specific questions for me, I will try and address them here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the point of Raeesah Khan, again, I was quite careful not to say anything which would get into the investigation per se, which is still ongoing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the matter here is about the point the Prime Minister raised about sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Prime Minister believes that it is appropriate to respond sensitively, given the circumstances at hand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And the point I was making was we were dealing here with someone who said she had been raped, and I did not sense that sensitivity coming from the PAP at that time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is the point I was trying to make.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On other matters, I think there will be further questions from WP MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I may come in and follow up with more questions in due course.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When the Leader of the Opposition spoke just now on a point of order, he said, or he claimed he was doing no more than the PAP MPs in making extended speeches with respect to the previous matter, which I think was the Ridout Road matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I was present for that debate, and I recall quite distinctly the PAP MPs, when seeking clarifications, did not make long speeches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Leader of the Opposition referred to Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Denise Phua asked a clarification, and it was directed obviously to the Prime Minister's Office.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministerial Statement was made by Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But because it is under Prime Minister's Office, the Prime Minister responded to that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When he responded, he was giving a response to the clarification and he can, therefore, give a longer answer.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He was not making a long speech on a clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Just a point of order and I wanted to clarify that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For a clarification on what he meant, because I am sure he does not mean it, but his statements are misleading on Ms Raeesah Khan.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My recollection was that the facts are as follows – and we need to be very clear on what the facts are when we speak in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I hope he can clarify and confirm that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, when someone stands up here and says, "We want to be sensitive", I think we need to look back at what each one did.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The word "rape" – my recollection was that it was insisted upon by Mr Singh.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was a serious matter – lying in Parliament – serious enough for her to be out of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: September came, October came, she repeated the lie in front of Mr Singh and no correction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap sat on a disciplinary panel to decide why Ms Khan did not tell the truth and sacked her.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if she was telling the truth that she had told them, and they admit they had been told, well, the public can judge for themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I think we should be very careful about putting out the facts.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I believe when the Prime Minister said – and he will speak for himself – about sensitivity, it is about how it affects everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I think if we had applied the same degree of sensitivity, no one would have insisted on recording that Ms Khan was raped.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But what I would say, and this is what I said in my first comment to the Prime Minister was, it is about the selective standard that is applied.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is normal for the PAP to say, "Look, be sensitive when a matter of this natures comes up." In referencing the word "rape", my point was this was how serious the matter was for us, as leaders to think about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I believe I was asked at the COP, "Why didn't you respond earlier?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Why didn't you react earlier?" And I said I should have reacted earlier but because I have an MP who had made such a serious point something of a personal nature, I also needed to make sure that she had addressed the matter with her parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because, in the words of the Prime Minister, you have to look at the circumstances and the spouses' and the families' conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think the Minister for Law is missing the point here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was not an insistence because of a lack of sensitivity vis-à-vis the word "rape".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was the circumstances we were in to make a decision in double quick time on what to do going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure what the second clarification was from the Law Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If he can repeat it, I will deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think everyone could see why that was done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She could have come up and said, "I didn't tell the truth" and her seniors in the party could have advised her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a matter that the COP had gone into extensively and it is a matter, some of it, that is now the subject of investigations.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members, I just want to remind everyone that today's Ministerial Statement concerns Minister Iswaran and the resignations of former Speaker and a PAP MP.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Again, let me just read out Standing Order 23 for everyone's benefit: "A statement may be made by a Minister in Parliament on the matter of public importance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members may seek clarification on the statement but no debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No debate shall be allowed thereon." Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think on the first point, I have stated the difference of opinion I have with the Minister for Law with regard to the use of the word and the reason why the word was important in the context of what the COP were investigating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the second point about mental illness, this is a question of fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We recorded it in our notes when she shared her condition and I felt that it was an important point for the COP to consider.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was not a case of putting someone with such an issue out to dry, as the Minister is very enthusiastic to portray.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second clarification about lying in Parliament, I think I dealt with this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I was not going to stand up and call her out and say, "No, these are the reasons why that lie had to be said." I think I made that apparent to the COP.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Vivian Balakrishan, you wanted to make a clarification?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I just wanted to address Mr Pritam Singh's suggestion that we had somehow been tardy or reticent with information with respect to TraceTogether.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I do not want this to become a whole repeat of an extended discussion which we had on this matter.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When I first was involved with the design of the system, it was purely for the purposes of contact tracing, dealing with the clear and present danger that COVID-19 presented to our population.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I made a statement – I think it was in June 2020 – which omitted four important words.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The four missing words which I said before was "subject to prevailing legislation".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Anyway, I made that statement in ignorance of the prevailing legislation, and I omitted those four words in June 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Round about, I believe, near the end of October 2020, a member of the public wrote to me and said, "Are you sure?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Please check." So, I said thank you and I did get my staff to check.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When my staff in the Smart Nation Office then told me actually, section 20 of the CPC may be relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That is when you will recall I said in this House, right from this stand, I had many sleepless nights deciding what we do about this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Or do we instruct the Police, or could we even instruct the Police, to proscribe their access to this data, although legally speaking, they have?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, there were sleepless nights on my part; intense discussions internally between multiple agencies on part of the Government in November 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And my staff will also recall I told them, whatever it is, when we finish this internal review, we will come back here, and we will come clean in my usual fashion and explain the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have taken some pains and I am sorry to take up the time, but I hope Mr Singh will realise that I have never deliberately engaged in any obfuscation, prevarication or delay.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have at all times acted in good faith.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have tried to make sure that in design, in execution and in coordination of a complex matter in an emergency, I have been transparent and forthright with the people and I object to your characterisation and use of an old debate which was settled in Parliament to suggest that there is a pattern of delay, prevarication and obfuscation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Leong Mun Wai had asked the Minister, "When did you discover that your statement was going to be affected by the CPC?" Minister did not answer that question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point here is there were Ministers who were in this House who knew that actually they were already in receipt of knowledge in October 2020 about the fact that TraceTogether applied to the CPC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But that was a month later in February, if I recall correctly, February 2021, where the Minister said – let me pull out the Hansard – I may just have a bit of it here when it was checked: "At the end of October..." – these are Minister Vivian's words – "...when I was asked basically what did I spend November doing?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As I said, double checking the legislation and then having, among sleepless nights and conversations, asking: 'Do we carve it out?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How do we do it?' So, that occupied us in November." That is what you said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I am saying is that there is a significant delay in time before answers are given by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Was Minister Vivian the only one looking at TraceTogether and the applicability of TraceTogether in May of 2020?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I also told my staff we will clear all these, whichever way it falls.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: A question was asked by Mr Christopher de Souza in December.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I do not think I delayed or obfuscated and, at all times, I have always been upfront and clean.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I mean, I have been here long enough.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, that is why I am objecting to your insinuation that there was any undue delay or any attempt at obfuscation or lack of transparency.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is not the way we do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I pulled up what the Committee said since Mr Singh has made reference to it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we should have on record what exactly happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just used that word..." – meaning "rape" – "... because that was the word Raeesah Khan used." Mr Edwin Tong says, "Yes, and I would prefer not; that we don't go into any other details unless they are strictly necessary." Mr Singh says, "I don't really know the details." Chairman says, "I am quite happy if you can just use 'sexual assault'." Mr Singh then said, "Okay, I will use 'sexual assault'.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just remember that, on record, that was what Ms Khan told us, that she was raped when she was 18." Then, on the other point on mental health, this is what the COP report says: "In the course of their testimony before the Committee, Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal made some assertions about Ms Khan's mental condition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that Ms Khan might be suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and disassociation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh said that on 4 October when he met Ms Khan in the Leader of Opposition's (LO) office, she was in a dazed state, suggesting that she was somewhat disoriented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Lim also gave the evidence that at the DP hearing on 29 November, Ms Khan explained that the anecdote was not in the first draft because she was disassociated and did not know what she was doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Lim also said that she was worried because as far as she and senior Workers' Party (WP) leaders could understand, Ms Khan was doing things without thinking." "Mr Singh also said that the statement in Ms Khan's 8 August WhatsApp message – 'they've agreed that the best thing to do is to take the information to the grave' – was a lie.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When Mr Singh was asked why Ms Khan would lie about this, Mr Singh said that Ms Khan had told the DP on 29 November that she suffered from disassociation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that Ms Khan may have a problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His position was that Ms Khan could be predisposed to lying because she had mental health issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh asked the Committee to consider asking Ms Khan to go for psychological assessment." "When Mr Singh was asked to explain his earlier evidence that there was nothing unusual about Ms Khan's performance as a Member of Parliament between August and September which was in contrast to his evidence that she could be suffering from disassociation, Mr Singh confirmed again that there was nothing out of the ordinary about Ms Khan's performance as a Member of Parliament at the material time." "Ms Khan was given an opportunity to respond to the assertions made by the three senior Workers' Party leaders regarding her mental health.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh had tried to paint a picture of her as someone who was mentally unstable when she was of sound mind." "In addition, Ms Khan had told the DP on 29 November that whilst her therapist had said that she might have symptoms of PTSD, she clarified that this was not something she was going through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mental health issues had to be approached with sensitivity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She expressed concern that using a person's mental health to discredit them, as Mr Singh and Ms Lim had done, would set back the movement to progress mental health awareness and support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Attributing such labels on people would discourage them from seeking help when they needed it." And, Sir, on the record is also expert testimony that Ms Khan did not have those issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third point is, Mr Singh, the Leader of Opposition, suggesting that I knew – because let us not make innuendos – that I knew of Mr Vivian Balakrishnan's statement and deliberately kept quiet?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call on the Leader of the Opposition, I want to again remind Members of today's Ministerial Statement and there are 12 Members who had filed PQs on this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: First, on the point that Minister Shanmugam raised on item 7294, that is my direct testimony and it does not contradict anything that I have said here today or make the point that the Minister is trying to suggest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He is referring not to my words or my testimony in the Committee, but how the COP characterised in its report, its interpretation of what had happened vis-à-vis what Ms Khan had said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But would the COP not want to know all the facts of the matter?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, in the documents that I submitted to the COP, it was clearly stated in my notes that this is what Raeesah Khan told us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And so, I was merely relaying that to the Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To then – as he is doing now – make an inductive leap and characterise that this is now an attack on all people who are suffering from mental health issues and that we are going for the jugular here, I think that is really, really not proper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think you have any basis to say that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The final point about innuendo and suggestions, my question to the Minister is this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will now request Members who have filed PQs earlier on this matter, if they have clarifications, to raise them.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I seek a bit of brief indulgence from Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I filed all three of my Oral Questions on the CPIB case and I hope Speaker will allow me to just ask three clarifications to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in hindsight, would that have possibly shaped CPIB's assessment of whether to disclose upfront that the Minister had himself been arrested, rather than stating in the initial press release that he was assisting with investigations?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My second clarification, without prejudging the issues, pertains to the Public Service Division (PSD).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the event that CPIB makes adverse findings against a particular public officer in the Public Service, will that public officer's previous official decisions be subject to retrospective review to ensure that there has not been any inappropriate influence swaying the decision?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, some may call recent events the reputational crisis of a generation for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Prime Minister and Government assure us and our residents that every effort will be made to repair the damage to Singapore's reputation so that people, businesses and others around the world will know that Singapore is going to settle the matter and put things right, because if we become just another ordinary country, Singapore will be finished.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will answer on behalf of the Prime Minister as this relates to the CPIB technical issues, which I thought we will address in the second bucket of questions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, will CPIB or, for that matter, any law enforcement agencies take a retrospective review of all decisions made by any officers being investigated?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is a decision entirely dependent on the investigations required by the respective law enforcement agencies, including CPIB.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, on Dr Tan Wu Meng's characterisation that this is a reputational crisis, as the Prime Minister said, "Yes, we have taken a hit", but I have always believed this – circumstances do not define us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our responses to circumstances define us and how we respond to circumstances will define us and we have every determination that the way we handle this must restore confidence, by the Singaporean public and our international partners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is some confusion, and I think the public will also like to know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We did read somewhere, from some mainstream media, that it was on 11 July.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But from what Minister Chan said just now, he seems to give the impression that the formal arrest was not taken until after 12 July.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And as the investigation progressed, CPIB made the relevant operational judgements on what to reveal.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if this is the case, which are the classes of people or public officers where the Prime Minister's concurrence is required, and under which section of the Prevention of Corruption Act is this specified?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And secondly, in relation to that, based on the provisions in the current statutes, should the Prime Minister and President both refuse to give concurrence to the CPIB, does it mean that the CPIB cannot commence formal investigations into certain classes of people?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Has the Prime Minister ever denied CPIB permission to conduct any investigation throughout its history?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the second answer to Mr Louis Chua's question is that: what if the Prime Minister and the President do not concur?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I know this is not currently required under the Prevention of Corruption Act, but I am just wondering, given that we have a slightly different approach with the commencement of investigations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I am just wondering whether this will also be the case.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And then secondly, I wanted to know if CPIB apprised the Prime Minister or other political office holders, Cabinet Ministers, about the facts relating to the active investigation into Minister Iswaran?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And whether or not any information about evidence was given and whether this was used in deciding whether or not to place Minister Iswaran on interdiction?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will check that and I will get back to the House.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First is on the matter of principle in my Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I asked about the transparent guidelines for mandatory disclosures or announcements when a Minister is personally implicated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am concerned first as a matter of principle, because a political office holder is involved and also in the context and environment that we are possibly open to leaks and the social media age that we are in, what does that mean in that sort of context?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does it really mean that we actually have to have a different set of rules or transparent guidelines when a political office holder or Minister is involved?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In normal circumstances, we would expect someone with interdiction from duty and no role or duties that would be undertaken for the month, would be taking an absence of leave from duty rather than possibly getting the $8,500?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Prime Minister can help answer the question.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In this case, CPIB judged and I supported them, that they are going to be interviewing a Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They are going to be interviewing other people, word would go around town.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is untenable for us to say we have no comment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And therefore, they put out the statement that they are interviewing a Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There have been, and it is not the previous precedent; those of you who are old enough to remember, I do not think there is anybody else in the House except me who was here when Mr Teh Cheang Wan was investigated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because you do not know at first, when you interview him, whether or not there is something there.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if you interview him, if you announce that he is being interviewed, Minister for National Development, and then it turns out there is nothing there, and you come out three days later and say, "the Minister for National Development is innocent", I think you are going to cause great consternation and, at the end of that, his reputation will be damaged undeservedly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But if you investigate him first, if it turns out there is something there, at some point, you cross a threshold and it is necessary to make an announcement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But would they know where the investigation will lead?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Three days later, after interviewing different people and establishing various facts, they make a fresh assessment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At that point, they are comfortable to say that the Minister was arrested and bailed, because the situation is different.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, these are operational judgements which our law enforcement agencies have got to make.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: All the law enforcement agencies, whether it is Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), whether it is the Police, whether it is CPIB.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Did they know that three days later, HPL would issue such a statement?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think they expected that HPL would have to issue such a statement because there is a regulatory requirement by the Singapore Exchange (SGX).

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not think they would know what Mr Ong Beng Seng would say and it would depend on what had transpired during the three days before Mr Ong put out that statement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I think, we are reading a lot into very little.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: First of all, nobody knew that Mr Iswaran might or might not have been doing something wrong.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Nobody raised a public scandal, no Parliamentary Questions in Parliament, not even from the WP.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But CPIB found out and they told me, and they decided to investigate the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It reached the point where they needed to interview the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And then, they came to tell me and say, "Can I have your concurrence?" Because CPIB reports to somebody.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Once upon a time, we had an SAF officer who went overseas on a course.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And the course mate asked him: "How do you keep your system clean, in Singapore, of corruption?" This is a country which grapples with this problem.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And he explained how we do it, we have the CPIB, it was zealous, it has a fearsome reputation, you go and "lim kopi", you know what will happen.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And his course mate asked him, "Whom does the CPIB report to?" So, he thought this was an organisational question.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, he said, "Well, it is independent, it has got its own chain of command, it reports to the Prime Minister." And his course mate looked at him again and says, "Who does the CPIB report to?" Why did he ask that question?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because the question, at the root of it, is the age-old problem – who is to judge the people who judge the people who judge the judges?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If the President agrees with the Prime Minister that the Director of CPIB does not have a case or has gone rogue, or is doing something ill-founded and says no, well, that is how two keys work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: No, because the Prime Minister may be corrupt, the President may be mistaken.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But it is as best, it is possible to contrive a system with human beings, which will work, provided you put honest people in charge.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is how the system is supposed to work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is unusual for a Prime Minister to have to do this to a Minister, but we are not the first organisation to confront this problem of a person under suspicion being investigated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And what do you do with him while he is being investigated, before he is either cleared or charged and convicted?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the case of the Ridout Road bungalows, I had no doubt I could leave the Ministers at work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I did not believe that they were guilty, neither did any evidence come up during the process of investigation that they were.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If the investigation had surfaced something which looked questionable, I would have been told and I would have made the decision on whether they needed to be interdicted and put on leave of absence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, they had some basis to come to some conclusion and I had to decide what to do with a Minister who is being investigated for what could be quite a serious matter, which is a possible corruption offence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because I do not have a precedent, I do not have a norm, I look at what the Civil Service does as a guideline.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But here, you have an officer who is under suspicion, who is under investigation, he has not been convicted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I could technically have said, "Well, presumed innocent and he goes on leave, full pay, until the matter is cleared." I could also have said, "There is a cloud.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I straightaway do not want anybody with a cloud.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: You are out." I think that would have been unjust because he has not been charged.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If there is a case, the case has not been heard, he has not been found guilty or acquitted or whatever.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I cannot prejudge a case based on an incomplete investigation – started recently, or a partial investigation, just entered into the formal phase.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think that is the proper way to do things.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After the receipt of this information, did the Prime Minister allow Minister Iswaran to continue his normal duties as Minister for Transport and MP for West Coast GRC?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It appears that the investigation on this case involving Minister Iswaran started some time before July, when the formal investigation was started.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask what is the difference between an investigation and a formal investigation by CPIB and when is this threshold crossed?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Concerning the vacation of the seat of the former Speaker, can I ask the Prime Minister, did the Parliamentary seat of the former Speaker become vacant in February 2023 when he offered his resignation to the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister accepted his resignation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, the Speaker of Parliament is supposed to be impartial towards all MPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Prime Minister did a conflict of interest occur due to the extramarital affair between the former Speaker and an MP when this information was not revealed to the House earlier on?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What is the difference between an informal, quiet investigation and a formal investigation?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In a quiet investigation, the CPIB does not exercise all of its powers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For example, it does not arrest people and formally interview them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
