text: It makes inquiries, it asks for information, but it has not formally exercised its powers to arrest a person and to compel him to answer their questions under the Prevention of Corruption Act, because under the Prevention of Corruption Act, if you answer the CPIB and give the CPIB a false answer, that is a crime.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, when you go into a formal investigation, a transition point is passed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The reason they needed to go into a formal investigation is because they had reached a point where they had to interview the principal parties who were involved, namely, Mr Iswaran.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They also had to interview several other people, including Mr Ong Beng Seng.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, they needed to launch a formal process at that point.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Taken strategically, the actual implementation was to come at a time convenient to me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, it is not a matter where you can stop having the affair and carry on as if nothing happened.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But neither is it a situation where the Speaker is in a position of command or supervisory responsibility over the MP.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Speaker presides, yes, but the Speaker is not the MPs' boss.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Speaker does not decide the MPs' bonus.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Speaker does not decide the MP's postings, does not assign work to the MPs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, therefore, you are in a situation where it is awkward, but it is not something which must be stopped immediately.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is why I asked you to think, have a thought experiment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Would it have been okay if the Speaker is married to a MP?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We have had a Minister married to a MP, both serving simultaneously in the House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Speaker and an MP serving in the House – is there anything wrong?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Speaker will have to be extra careful and make sure that he will bend over backwards not to be seen to be favouring his wife or her husband.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But if it is an extramarital affair, I think that is different.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It puts everybody else on edge, in an awkward position – MPs as well as staff.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In Singapore's context, people look at it and say, this will not pass muster.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, that is a situation we are in.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is not a question of my making a conflict of interest decision where I am making a decision which financially benefits me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But it is a situation where a personal relationship crosses with a public relationship.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In this case, it is an extramarital personal relationship and that makes it difficult.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sorry, let Minister Chan make his response first.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Any code of conduct will lay out the broad principles and the guidelines for people to follow, but they must be complemented by good people who must abide by the spirit of the rules and not just the letter of the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this is how we run our system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Three things: we need good rules, we need good people, and if any of these things fail, we must have the third limb, which is that we must have a system to make sure that we put things right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, in setting out any rules or code of conduct, we are mindful that the rules must be clear, yet, at the same time, not so prescriptive until it becomes paralysing for the system to work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second step – it is very important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is to have good people with good values who can interpret the rules, abide by the rules and the spirit of the rules, and, if something goes wrong, we must have the system to put it right.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My question is to Minister Chan, and it pertains to my Question No 11.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Public Service intend to strengthen its whistle-blowing policies and promote better awareness of these policies so that civil servants are protected by non-retaliation policies that are in place?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will just add that the Public Service will continue to make sure that our rules are relevant and current to the circumstances and needs of the time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to do this regularly to make sure that our rules are updated, that our people are kept updated and that they have the confidence to do what is right.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: First, to revisit the question about why Minister Iswaran's leave of absence is not no-pay leave.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The Prime Minister mentioned that in the Civil Service, the practice is to put them on half pay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I can understand the rationale for that in the case of low-wage earners who may need a regular monthly income in order to survive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But I think that hardly applies in the case of a Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: For $8,500 a month, that might be small change to some, but many Singaporeans have to work very hard for much less than that.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Although the Minister said that there is a non-retaliation clause, can the Minister elaborate on what that non-retaliation clause comprises or, if not, to let me know where I can find further information on that?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the spirit of the non-retaliation law and it is in our Public Service rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Sorry, Mr Speaker, to respond to Ms Poa on why not no pay leave.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Here, I have to be fair to the Minister involved as well as do the right thing by the Government and the taxpayer.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He is under investigation, it is not a minor matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Is it fair for me to say, "Your pay goes to zero"?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I think we have to go on principles, rather than whatever we do, anything you can do, I can do stronger.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think that would not be a wise approach to take.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This question is in relation to Minister Chan's earlier comment in relation to CPIB being functionally independent.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My clarification is, what oversight is exercised over the CPIB and whether the CPIB's investigation methods are being audited on a regular basis to ensure impartiality and parity of treatments, regardless of the identity of the subject of their investigations?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They also learn from best practices from other parts of the world to make sure that our systems are up to mark.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the most significant test of whether our investigations are up to mark is really this – that when CPIB or any of our law enforcement agencies submit their case to the AGC and it goes to the Courts, are our investigation methods up to the mark?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because if they are not up to the mark, they will be rejected by the AGC and the Courts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the final arbiter, if you like, of the quality of the work that our law enforcement agencies do is actually our Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier, the Prime Minister said that sometime after 29 May, the Prime Minister had informed someone in MTI.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My second clarification for the Prime Minister is, the Prime Minister mentioned about the interdiction and how he arrived at the pay of $8,500.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Just a quick clarification – is this in lieu of both Minister's pay and MP's allowance?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Speaker, Sir, I do not think it was a very difficult question to figure out, that when I spoke to MTI, I spoke to the Minister, because Mr Gan Kim Yong is the Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Iswaran has a role in MTI, he is overseeing various matters to do with trade as well as projects like the Formula One (F1) and I thought it was important that the Minister for MTI knows that there is an investigation going on concerning Mr Iswaran, so that he knows how to deal with the issue until the investigation has reached a point and the matter is public.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The MP's allowance is different from the pay, it is not at the discretion of the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If you want to do that, Parliament has to move a Motion to interdict the MP as an MP and Parliament has not done that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And neither in previous cases, has Parliament done that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What has happened is that the MP has been on a leave of absence, and eventually when the case is settled one way or the other, well, then, consequences follow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A Motion would have to be moved in Parliament to suspend the Member from the service of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: His or her allowance would be withheld thereafter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Ms He Ting Ru's second question, can you repeat your second question, or the second part of your question?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think the question that I asked was, did CPIB apprise the Prime Minister or any other Cabinet Minister about the facts relating to the investigation to Minister Iswaran and including information about evidence that became available?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Director of CPIB only apprised the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms He Ting Ru, I assume you had raised your hand earlier, was that the clarification wanted?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the event that a Permanent Secretary or a director or a chief executive of a Statutory Board is being invited to assist with any investigation, will he or she be asked to take a leave of absence?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The PSD together with the head of Civil Service and if need be, the Minister in charge of the Public Service will have to make a decision in context.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not think Prime Minister has answered the question as to why it took so long to make arrangements to hand over the residents of Kembangan-Chai Chee to others in Marine Parade GRC, from February to July.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He has not answered why it takes so long.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification is that I wonder whether he will agree with me that the period from February to July actually was quite momentous, many things happened in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We had Budget debate, Committee of Supply, Parliament was prorogued, Parliament reopened.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There were Sittings in April and May, and some of us even went with the former Speaker on official trips overseas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, does he not think that this inordinate delay to settle the matter is really highly regrettable, because it gives a false impression to all of us here, to the general public and even to the outside world?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have three clarifications, two of them pertain to the practicality and sustainability of ensuring that there can always be good talent in our politics and the last question pertains to the threats to the trust and the social compact between our citizens and the Government.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As I need to give some context to these questions, may I beg your indulgence for a little time?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: And the reality of an MP's life is that we often disappoint our spouses or children who may be waiting at home on the weekends, or at night when we get held back at work, at events, at contingencies in the constituency.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Tan, I would appreciate if you would go straight to your clarification.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So my question is, how can we make political representation more sustainable and family-friendly in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: And two, sharing a little bit of personal context, I personally would not have decided to enter politics in 2020 if I had not by then found a partner that I planned to settle down with.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, for any political candidate who is still single and have not yet found a life partner upon entering politics, the fact of life is, it is really hard to date or to find potential partners.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, is it possible that we can allow politicians some space for their personal lives away from public scrutiny, just for the sake of ensuring that there will always be willing and capable candidates, albeit single, willing to serve as politicians without being in reality, doomed to singlehood pretty much, until they are past their prime?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: The third point is, the Internet is rife with a lot of false information and opportunistic narratives, and the way algorithms on social media platforms push info onto our feeds also perpetuate personal bias and social polarisation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: As much as there are many young people who are quite discerning about this, there are a vast majority who are rather passive consumers of certain narratives and information.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: So, what can we do to better protect our young citizens from being confounded by social media consumption that has the power to cause disillusionment or apathy towards the system?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: Again, this is a point that I would like us to consider and seek leadership guidance on the prevention of cynicism and apathy from setting into Singapore society towards our political system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think we can understand where the Member is coming from.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have clear rules of propriety and probity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They do not conflict with the aspirations for our personal and family lives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know the public's expectations for public figures are high.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where we fall short, we seek to improve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where we have done well, we must remain vigilant and not complacent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, the will to answer the call to serve is deeply personal.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I agree, we can all do our part to encourage a positive political environment and engender a more constructive political culture so that we do not deter good people from stepping forth to serve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe in Brazil, for example, the so-called Car Wash investigations actually reported to judges, as well as possibly a legislature.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I hope that it portends a change in your attitude towards the Elected President and his custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I think the Brazil example is a very interesting one.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, the code of conduct is always revised at the start of every new administration, and there is a setting out of the possible sanctions as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Code of Conduct for Ministers be similarly reviewed more consistently, and perhaps, the sanctions available to be expressly stated for any breaches?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second point is that we take the point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to regularly review the Ministerial Code of Conduct and all the other regulations that safeguard our system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third point follows on from what the Prime Minister has said, and I think I have also shared this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But ultimately, the rules, by themselves, cannot be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need good people – good people that will abide by the spirit of the rules; good people that will interpret the rules; and not people that will try to go around the rules.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In my mind, I think in our political culture, the ultimate sanction is not whether someone has committed a mistake and pays a certain fine or others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The ultimate sanction is what will the public think of us as legislators, as part of the leadership team of this country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we must do what we can to uphold the standards whether the sanctions are codified or not codified.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask Minister Chan, Minister Iswaran was put on leave of absence since 6 July, if I am right.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Oh, no, no; that was his personal leave of absence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, the Prime Minister knows that the CPIB has been investigating him informally since May, but the formal investigation would start after getting concurrence from the Prime Minister, on 5 April.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he was on personal leave of absence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And then, during the period of personal leave of absence, he represented Singapore to meet the Chief Minister of Johor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These kind of practices — you know, I fully support what the Leader of Opposition said just now about the standards of Government, about delays, about indecisions and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If you already knew the Minister has been under investigation for so many months, why did you still let him go and represent Singapore to meet up with the Chief Minister of Johor?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we use the word "investigations", I think the Prime Minister and myself have gone through the different stages of investigations and what are the associated actions that we may take in accordance with the needs of that stage of investigation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It does not mean that just because somebody is under investigation, all things will follow immediately.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I hope we have made that clear in our presentation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the context of how the Prime Minister has judged what duties Minister Iswaran can undertake at different stages of the investigation process.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, a short clarification, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, Sir, with due respect, sorry, I still have quite a number of questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I will ask one more question first, okay?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But by having all these delays in taking the decisive actions, do you not think that this is not in line with the Government's stance of zero tolerance towards corruption?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The moment a Minister is investigated, even informally, I think more decisive action should be taken.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Information comes up, a Minister is quietly being investigated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Should I straightaway tell the Minister, "By the way, CPIB is quietly investigating you, please have a care"?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Supposing I say: "You go on leave of absence".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is my duty to make sure that while he is working and, knowing that there is a cloud, he does not make any steps which are going to dig the hole further or cause a problem.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if something like that threatens to come up, I will have to find some way to head it off.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Why does CPIB need time to get ready for a formal investigation?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because they must have all the facts and evidence enough to start interviewing the principal person.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Otherwise, if you go in and the principal person turns up and you have announced that you have arrested him and then it turns out that there is nothing in the case, I think you have been derelict in your duty.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, you must make sure, as much as possible, that the case is there before you go to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And when do you go to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What else do they want to do at the same time?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I defer to them on these operational judgements.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I said the timing is entirely up to you.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And that is all there is to it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The reason this is here at all is because this Government decided to act – "ownself check ownself".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is how the system is meant to work and that depends on the leadership, on the Government, on the whole ethos of our society, to frown on corruption, to have no tolerance for somebody who falls short of the standards we expect.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And when something needs to be done, painful or not, we do it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If it has to be done, it has to be done.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They will do their job and, in due course, everything will be settled.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I think that is the way we keep Singapore working for a long time to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I would also suggest if you have a few questions, ask all of them at one go.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I respect what the Prime Minister said just now with regard to the stance of the current Government, but I would also like to make a point that if our current system is not "ownself check ownself", but there are more checks and balances, perhaps, there will not be delays in all these things.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, I will ask two more questions to the Prime Minister which are important for our Motion debate afterwards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I confirm with the Prime Minister that, with regard to Speaker Tan's case, what the Prime Minister is saying now is that in February this year, he did not actually accept the resignation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Basically, he is saying that the resignation is put on hold and you carry on doing what you need to do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because if you have accepted the resignation and then you allowed Speaker Tan to continue to perform certain duties, I do not know, the legal colleagues and Members in this Chamber may have other questions that can be raised pertaining to this issue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, this one point I would like to confirm so that I can say the right thing during the debate on the Motion afterwards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second point, can the Prime Minister confirm that he would not have asked Speaker Tan to resign, even after the revelation of those offensive comments that he had made in Parliament, if Speaker Tan had not been in an inappropriate relationship with an MP?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In terms of the decision made – I have decided, he has decided.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Would I have asked him to resign if it was just a matter of the hot mic?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It was wrong for him to say that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It was bad that it was picked up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: No Member should say that in the House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Dare I say no Member should say that even outside of the House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I hazard to guess that maybe not all of us abstain completely all the time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But we do expect standards of behaviour in this House and especially in the Chair.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is not new, and it is a further clarification, I assume?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, I would really appreciate it if you would ask all your questions, because there are still a few more hands, and I just want to give everyone an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And if not, will the Police conduct any investigation to determine if any laws were broken?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose the question, I think, is directed indirectly to me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just want to understand the provision so that we can be clearer, then I can answer the question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just tried to pull it up as he was speaking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, in reply to the Minister, actually I do not have the specific section of the Private Security Act, with regard to private investigation and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But as a layman, I am just concerned that anyone of us in the public space can be secretly taken, you know, and it is —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I can have that, then I can proceed to answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, Speaker, then I would say that I do not have the provision.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But can I ask for a general opinion from the Home Affairs Minister, whether such an act of secretly taking the video of other citizens, how is it covered under our law because it is an intrusion into the privacy of the individual?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say, Sir, through you, that if Mr Leong and the PSP believes that there should be no videos taken of anyone, as a matter of procedure and law, perhaps he can table a Private Member's Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because, as far as I am aware today, there is no legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last Saturday, PSP came to my constituency, as is usual, they sat in a corner and had their coffee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, I did my usual walkabout and PSP sent someone to video me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, they did not think that they were breaking any laws and I have a photograph of that if Mr Leong wishes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, certainly, your party does not think that there is anything wrong in constantly videoing us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you believe that — I think if my recollection serves me right – Mr David Ong was an MP here and was subject to a private investigator's video by the husband of the lady involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think on the reference to Private Security Industry Act, I would just say this, Sir, through you, which I have said before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a question is to be asked, we as Ministers have a duty to answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think, equally, MPs have a duty to do some basic checks before they throw questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, if you referred to a legislation, then tell us which provision you are referring to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, something must have gone through your mind that the Private Security Industry Act is relevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not see anything there that is relevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, maybe, I thought you knew something that I did not know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it appears that, perhaps, you know even less even though you ask the question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think it would be a waste of very important Parliamentary time if MPs do not do some basic research.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is all I have to say, Sir.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not believe any section of the Private Security Industry Act applies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: To the Prime Minister and, perhaps, to Mr Chan as well, I think the issue of whether the Prime Minister's concurrence is required for any CPIB investigation is an important question.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have tried to search for the legal basis for that, but I cannot find any section which actually says that the Director of CPIB has to get the Prime Minister's concurrence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Prevention of Corruption Act talks about seeking concurrence from the Public Prosecutor, but the Prime Minister is actually not mentioned in the legal provisions, as far as I can find.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, may I get clarification as to whether it is just customary because CPIB comes under the Prime Minister's Office, that is, CPIB would inform the Prime Minister of such?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Minister Chan did say he is going to make a clarification on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like to know when that will happen.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the second point I will make.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, as the Prime Minister enunciated just now, there are two keys: one, is the Prime Minister, whether he agrees; and then after that, the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, the question posed is, what if the Prime Minister and the President, both do not agree with the Director of CPIB, and I think the Prime Minister has made that clear.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I just want to make these points on record.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You want to ask a clarification to Mr Leong's comment about —

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Yes, Sir, and also, to clarify what Minister Shanmugam had said about the Private Security Industry Act.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I am asking the question because I am the President of the Security Association Singapore, which also represents private investigators.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: So, the clarification that I wanted to make was whether Mr Leong was conflating the use of private investigators and the general taking of videos in public.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: The Private Security Industry Act does provide that in a security assignment or private investigation assignment involving a political figure which is defined as the President, the Prime Minister, a Minister or a Minister of State, then there is a requirement to get the approval from the licensing officer.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: But in other cases, which is what Minister Shanmugam mentioned, where there were people who took a video of him in public, there is really no need for that and the Private Security Industry Act would not apply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have a clarification for the Leader of the Opposition, arising from his earlier invitation, where he said he is prepared to answer any question about his party's handling of the indiscretion between his two party members.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is evidence in public of a video by Mr Perera's driver who said he had told Mr Singh as well as other MPs, including Ms Sylvia Lim and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, about the indiscretions Mr Perera was engaging in, including going to hotels, going to restaurants and so on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Could Mr Singh please tell this House why nothing was done at the material time?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second clarification is: were any steps taken to protect the identity of the driver as the informant?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first one, can I ask the Member in return, has he perused the entire press conference that was given by the WP on this matter, where the question was answered?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But I have not heard any explanation as to why the driver was not called up for an interview after those details were given.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We approached Mr Perera; I approached Mr Perera with the information that was given to me by the driver.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I had explained in my press conference what was said by Mr Perera to me and our assessment at the time was, this was what had transpired.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But if the Member had listened to the press conference carefully, and I do not think he did, other facts came to bear, such as corroboratory evidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think a Stomp article suggested that this video was the video that came out on the same day that the Prime Minister was announcing the resignation of the Speaker and Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Stomp reported that the video had been going around since 2021.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I can confirm because I asked the Central Executive Committee (CEC) the question, my CEC, had anybody seen the video.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Perhaps, he can tell me if he had.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If either of these two criteria came into play, then I think something different would have happened.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We would have to look into the matter more carefully, beyond what Mr Perera had shared with us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In terms of protecting the identity of the source, I did not reveal the identity of the source, but I had to check with Mr Perera, "This is the information I received.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I can confirm that I did not see the video before it was all over the public domain, but I have a few further clarifications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Do you not think that if you received credible evidence from someone who is close to an indiscretion – I mean a whistle-blower, this is how issues normally come up – that you should actually take efforts to interview the person to get more information?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The second is this: you mentioned that you did not tell Mr Perera or you did not reveal the source of information.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How did you tell Mr Perera you came to know about this indiscretion?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But on the first point – can you just repeat the first point, the first question?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The first question was, if you receive information from a credible source who is close to the wrongdoing that something has happened, normally, in a proper organisation, that would be treated as a whistle-blower report.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Steps would be taken to protect that person and that person would be called up for further interviews.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Was this driver called up for a further interview?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As I mentioned in my first reply, we had to deal with the information that was shared by the driver, we made an assessment of the total circumstances with which the information was provided to us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And as we found out – after the fact of course – this person was a former police officer with more than I think 10 years' experience, I think this was in the papers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would have expected somebody close to Mr Perera, very close to Mr Perera to have corroboratory evidence at hand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I would have expected that, especially being a driver.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I think Mr Singh has not answered my question which was, did he call him up for an interview?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Was it conveyed to him that he needed to collate further corroboratory evidence?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, you have a clarification.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Earlier, he had said something about if an MP is under investigation, he expected the Government to do something about it.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, can I ask Mr Leong to clarify, is it his position that if any MP is under police investigation, we should then suspend the MP or dock his salary?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would expect our Government's stance on zero tolerance to include what I said just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That means once the Minister is under investigation, he should be relieved of his duties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But is it Mr Leong's position that the Leader of the Opposition cannot receive pay or carry out his duties because he is an MP?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Because, to me, surely, you must be convicted before something can happen.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Is Mr Leong saying that the minute a person is referred to the Police for investigation, the MP must be suspended, or he must receive a salary cut?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: And I just want to assure the Leader of the Opposition, that is not my position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, he also has said, "Leon also shared with me that he was in an ongoing dispute with his driver and was about to terminate his services and had sought legal advice on the allegations of his driver", and a few other statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think, just to be clear, Mr Singh's position is that he did not reveal the identity of the source – that is what he just told us – to Mr Perera.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think he was interested in protecting his identity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But insofar as the question directed to me, like I said, the conversation with Mr Perera, Mr Perera would have known who that individual was when I asked him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I did not actively go and seek to do something nefarious.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Patrick Tay, I hope your clarification is related to the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is a question for the Minister-in-charge of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think the recent spate of events has affected the morale of the Public Service officers and I want to hear from him what response he has as the Minister-in-charge of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am acutely aware that these recent developments that we discussed at length in the House today may have caused uncertainty and dented overall confidence in our Public Service and also among some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, I have received similar feedback from our Public Service officers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some wonder if the recent incidents had impacted confidence in our Government and, at the same time, created doubts in the work of our Public Service officers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Others have asked me if they can still do their jobs well and without fear, especially amidst greater scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I strongly believe – and I share this with my colleagues in the Public Service – that our work in the Public Service is not measured by the here and now, but over the long term.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also acknowledge like anyone else that we are not perfect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You can have my assurance that the Public Service will continue to learn from the recent episodes, apply the lessons and strive to do even better for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Introduction of Government Bills, Minister for Home Affairs.
